title: fxCheshire prototype: cat fades out, grin holds above the match
description:
FILE: artifacts/prototypes/effects-playground.html (prototype only — do NOT touch
extension/content.js in this bead).

AMENDED 2026-09-04: the blind fire-by-index harness is abandoned along with the Fable
5.1 round-6 candidates. This effect is fired from its LABELLED SIDEBAR BUTTON, not by
index. oculist-e2m.1 adds a new sidebar divider group for these two new candidates;
append to that group, do not let this land inside the retired "Round 6" group.

READ FIRST: fxCallout in the same file (an above-the-match element with placement
logic) and fxComet (the general conventions: viewport coordinates via baseStyle()'s
position:fixed, class "fx", mount(), a local var DUR, hardcoded colors). Read them for
their CONVENTIONS only — fxCallout is one of the abandoned round-6 candidates and is
not a design to imitate.

CONCEPT: a hand-drawn cartoon cat appears above the match, then its BODY fades away
while its wide toothy grin stays, pops, and only then fades. "Remains above the match"
means it outlasts the body — it must NOT persist indefinitely.

STEPS

1. Add `function fxCheshire(r)` alongside the other fx* functions. Build ONE inline
   SVG containing exactly two groups:
     - #cat: head outline, two ears, a few body stripes, whiskers, two eyes, a curled
       tail.
     - #grin: a wide crescent mouth arc plus a zigzag row of teeth across it.
   The grin must read clearly on its own once #cat is gone — that is the whole point
   of the effect, so give it enough weight (thicker stroke, larger arc) that it does
   not look like a leftover fragment.

2. Hand-drawn feel: stroke-linecap:round, stroke-linejoin:round,
   vector-effect:non-scaling-stroke, and deliberately slightly irregular control
   points (a hand-authored wobble, not Math.random() — the shape must be identical on
   every fire so scoring is repeatable).

3. Sizing and placement. Cat height = clamp(3.2 * r.height, 48, 110). Horizontally
   centred on the match. Sits ABOVE the match with an 8px gap. If
   r.top < catHeight + 8 there is not room above, so draw it BELOW the match instead
   and mirror the vertical drift in step 4 accordingly.

4. Timeline. Use ONLY opacity and transform — no filter, no blur on the moving parts.
   var DUR = 1500.
     - 0-180ms:    the whole SVG fades in, transform scale 0.9 -> 1.
     - 180-780ms:  #cat animates opacity 1 -> 0. #cat and #grin get SEPARATE
                   animations; #grin stays at opacity 1 throughout and translates
                   ~6px toward the match so it settles just above the match's top
                   edge as the body leaves.
     - 780-900ms:  #grin pops, scale 1.12 -> 1, transform-origin at the grin's own
                   centre. A brief glow pulse on the teeth (a box-shadow or an SVG
                   drop-shadow on the teeth path only) fades in and out across this
                   window. Gate the glow behind a `var LITE = false;` constant at the
                   top of the function — the shipped version will read
                   settings.performanceMode, and the prototype needs the degraded
                   look to be checkable by flipping one line.
     - 900-1500ms: #grin holds, then fades to opacity 0.

5. IMPORTANT, learned from oculist-e2m.1's review: the grin must not OCCLUDE the
   matched text. S2 (context preservation) is weighted x4 and S7 (anchor legibility)
   x2. The grin settles ABOVE the match's top edge, never over the glyphs.

6. Register it: `cheshire: { label: 'Cheshire', run: fxCheshire },` at the END of the
   playground's effectsRegistry, after the flappy entry from oculist-e2m.1. Do not
   reorder existing entries. Confirm it renders as a clickable labelled button in the
   new sidebar divider group, alongside Flappy.

DONE-CRITERIA
- Clicking the Cheshire button in the sidebar shows a recognisable cartoon cat that
  dissolves leaving only its toothy grin hovering above the match, which pops, holds,
  then fades — with the matched text never covered.
- With the match scrolled near the top of the viewport (less than catHeight + 8 px of
  room above it), the whole thing draws BELOW the match instead, still fully on screen.
- Nothing remains on the page after ~1.5s; clearFx() removes it (every element carries
  class "fx").
- Flipping LITE to true removes the teeth glow and nothing else.
- No page reflow, no mutation of #match or its text, no restorer needed.
- The #fire-index input and its max attribute are NOT touched.
close_reason: Cat fades to its grin above the match, tail dropped, no teeth glow. Reviewer PASS. Committed 982ec52.

title: fxFlappy prototype: physics-driven zigzag flight to the match
description:
FILE: artifacts/prototypes/effects-playground.html (prototype only — do NOT touch
extension/content.js in this bead).

READ FIRST: fxComet in the same file. It is the closest existing travel effect and
establishes every convention you must follow — viewport coordinates (elements are
position:fixed via baseStyle()), class "fx", mount(), a local var DUR, hardcoded
colors, and offset-path:path('...') driven by a WAAPI offsetDistance 0% -> 100%
animation. There is NO cursor tracking in the playground; fxComet derives its start
point from the viewport (nearest corner). Follow that.

STEPS

1. Add `function fxFlappy(r)` alongside the other fx* functions. Start point: the
   midpoint of whichever vertical viewport edge (left or right) is nearer the match
   centre, inset 40px — the same nearest-point idea fxComet uses for corners. End
   point: the match centre (r.left + r.width/2, r.top + r.height/2).

2. Generate the trajectory from physics, once, at fire time. There is no rAF loop.
   Declare two named tunables at the top of the function:
       var GRAVITY = <px per ms^2>;
       var FLAP_IMPULSE = <px per ms, upward, negative>;
   Integrate with a fixed step (16ms is fine): each step vy += GRAVITY * dt and
   y += vy * dt; every FLAP_PERIOD ms set vy = FLAP_IMPULSE outright (an
   instantaneous reset, NOT an added force — that reset is what makes the path a
   sawtooth of parabolic arcs rather than a sine wave). x advances linearly from
   start to end across the whole duration.

3. Flap count from distance: n = clamp(Math.round(dist / 160), 2, 6). Derive
   FLAP_PERIOD = DUR / n, then solve GRAVITY and FLAP_IMPULSE so that each arc sags
   about 34px and the integrated path lands within 2px of the end point. Correct any
   residual drift by adding a linear correction term across the samples so the final
   sample is exactly the end point — the bird must not miss the match.

4. Sample the trajectory into an SVG path string ("M x0 y0 L x1 y1 L ...") and set it
   as offset-path on the bird element, with offset-rotate:auto and
   offset-anchor:50% 50%. offset-rotate:auto makes the nose follow the velocity
   tangent, which is Flappy Bird's own rotation rule — do not hand-roll rotation
   keyframes.

5. Bird art: inline SVG, roughly 26px, ORIGINAL art (a round body, one wing, a beak
   triangle, an eye dot). Do NOT reproduce the Flappy Bird sprite. A single solid
   fill color is correct; the shipped version will take it from the beacon color.

6. Wing flap: the wing <path> gets its own WAAPI animation, a scaleY squash, with
   iterations: n and duration: FLAP_PERIOD, so the wing beat is synced to the arcs by
   construction rather than by a magic number.

7. Leftward travel: offset-rotate:auto would fly the bird upside-down when the start
   is to the RIGHT of the match. Apply scaleX(-1) on an inner wrapper element and add
   180deg to offset-rotate in that case. The playground's #match sits left of centre
   so the flight normally comes from the left; expose a `var FROM_RIGHT = false;`
   constant at the top of the function that forces the start to the right edge, so
   the mirrored case can be verified by flipping one line.

8. Degenerate case: if Math.abs(dx) < 120, ignore the computed start and launch from
   200px to the left of the match instead, so there is always a visible flight.

9. Arrival: the bird settles on the match's top edge (offsetDistance ends at 100%,
   then a short opacity fade), and an absorption flash fires on the match rect —
   copy the shape of the flash at the end of animateTrail in extension/content.js
   (rect inflated by 6px, opacity 0 -> 1 -> 0 with a scale 1 -> 1.15 -> 1, delayed by
   DUR so it can never fire before the bird lands).

10. Register it: `flappy: { label: 'Flappy', run: fxFlappy },` at the END of the
    playground's effectsRegistry object, so it takes index 39. Do not reorder
    existing entries — the score sheet indexes off this order.

DONE-CRITERIA
- Serving the playground over http://127.0.0.1:PORT/ and firing index 39 shows a bird
  flying a visible sawtooth of 2-6 parabolic arcs, nose tilting up on each flap and
  down on each fall, landing exactly on the match, followed by the flash.
- Flipping FROM_RIGHT to true flies it in from the right, right way up, facing left.
- Nothing remains on the page after the animation; clearFx() removes it (every
  element carries class "fx").
- No page reflow, no mutation of #match or its text, no restorer needed.
close_reason: Pixel-exact reproduction of the reference sprite, verified by extracting the cell grid back out of the rendered SVG. Physics, level landing and exact arrival previously reviewed and passed. Committed a1011ca.

title: Suite launch capacity: 51 of 58 files launch Chromium at concurrency 4, needs a load repro before pricing
description:
Split out of oculist-8ou on 2026-09-02, which covered only that bead's finding 1. Finding 1 is done and committed (c8db638); this is finding 2, untouched.

THE FACT: 51 of 58 test files call launchPersistentContext, and npm test runs at --test-concurrency=4. On an IDLE machine this produced launchPersistentContext Timeout 180000ms exceeded in beacon_fade_persistent_overlays.test.js:34, cascading into 2 cancelled tests (305 pass / 0 fail / 2 cancelled, 210.7s). A separate idle run went 297 pass / 2 fail / 8 CANCELLED at 300s.

WHY FINDING 1 DOES NOT COVER THIS, established by the oculist-8ou reviewer rather than assumed. The scaled action timeout applies to a context AFTER launchPersistentContext resolves. A launch that never returns is categorically outside its reach. Finding 1 is also a NO-OP at the default scale (30000 * 1 = 30000) and npm test never sets OCULIST_TEST_TIMEOUT_SCALE, so it changes nothing on an ordinary run at all. It is headroom for contended and CI runs with the knob turned up, nothing more.

DO THIS FIRST, AND DO NOT SKIP IT: REPRODUCE UNDER LOAD. Six consecutive quiet runs during the oculist-8ou review came back 307/0 at 75.4s to 77.3s, spread under 2 seconds. That is not a baseline against which 'materially tightened variance' can be measured, because there is no variance left to tighten in that sample. Pricing the options off quiet runs would be measuring nothing. Find a way to reproduce the launch failure reliably (deliberate parallel load, a constrained container, or a lower resource ceiling) before touching anything.

BE CAREFUL WITH THE OBVIOUS LEVER. Dropping --test-concurrency is easy but the test-suite-flake memory records concurrency 1 at 232-245s per run against roughly 75s at concurrency 4, so serializing costs about 3x on every run forever. That is a permanent developer-velocity cost paid to fix a failure mode that may only appear under load nobody normally creates. Measure, then choose.

OPTIONS TO PRICE, not to assume: lower --test-concurrency; give launchPersistentContext an explicit scaled timeout so the failure is at least attributable rather than an 180s stall; or reduce how many files need their own browser (the oculist-8ou reviewer noted 53 near-identical launch blocks with all four launch options identical, which is a real shared-helper candidate and would also make finding 1's monkeypatch unnecessary).

DONE WHEN: the launch failure is first reproducible on demand, then a chosen option is shown to fix it, with before and after measurements from the SAME load conditions. Note the durations and failing test names from every run; a prior measurement lost the failing test names by not piping output to a file.

Blocks oculist-67h, whose original 5s timeout in beacon_fade_persistent_overlays may simply disappear once launch contention is addressed.
close_reason: Premise did not survive the required load repro. The 180s launchPersistentContext hang never reproduced at any load level; synthetic CPU load produced a 2x slowdown and zero failures. Only concurrent suite invocations degraded it, and those failures were a different family. All three options priced against an untriggerable failure and rejected. Chris ruled concurrent suites out of scope 2026-09-02. Viewport-not-identical correction recorded for anyone sizing the shared-helper option later.

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text: Phase 1 measurement done (no code changed, git status clean). Summary: quiet baseline reconfirmed 307/0 at ~80s x2. CPU-spin load (yes-workers) up to 20 workers only slowed the suite 2x with zero failures — synthetic CPU contention does not reproduce this. Running 3 concurrent full 'npm test' invocations (matching the real oculist-67h confound) DID reproduce failure: 306/1, 306/1, 305/2 across the three, each a DIFFERENT test, none of them launchPersistentContext timeouts -- all were assertion-shaped race conditions in already-launched contexts (chip_row.test.js:360, list_search.test.js:371, instant_scroll_close_reopen_no_stale_draw.test.js:194+vision_profile_survives_ungoverned_toggle.test.js:57). Did not obtain the specific 180s launchPersistentContext timeout within time budget; that needs a heavier/longer load than 3-concurrent-suites produced in this attempt. Launch-block audit: 51 files call launchPersistentContext; headless/channel/args identical across all 51, but viewport is NOT identical (4 variants) and a few files add colorScheme/reducedMotion -- the 'all four options identical' premise is false as stated. Full numbers and recommendation in session report to orchestrator.

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
RESOLVED BY DECISION, 2026-09-02. Chris: 'One at a time is acceptable for now.'

This bead required a load repro BEFORE pricing, and was explicit that pricing off quiet
runs would be measuring nothing. The repro phase ran and the premise did not survive it.

WHAT WAS MEASURED (full run table in the previous comment):
- The headline failure, launchPersistentContext Timeout 180000ms exceeded, NEVER
  reproduced at any load level tested.
- Synthetic CPU load does not touch this failure mode at all. 8 and 20 spinners on a
  10-core box gave a 2x slowdown and ZERO failures. The load generator has to be more
  Chromium launches, not more CPU. That is the most useful finding here.
- Three concurrent npm test invocations DID degrade it: 306/1, 306/1, 305/2, a different
  test each run. But all five failures were assertion-shaped races inside ALREADY-LAUNCHED
  contexts, i.e. finding 1's territory (oculist-8ou, closed), not this bead's launch-
  capacity concern.

WHY IT CLOSES RATHER THAN STAYING OPEN. With concurrent suite runs ruled out of scope,
there is no condition under which the failure this bead names is known to occur. All
three options were priced against a failure nobody can trigger:
  (a) lower --test-concurrency: a permanent ~3x tax on every solo run, and it does not
      even address the mechanism observed, since concurrent INVOCATIONS each still launch
      their own herd. Rejected.
  (b) explicit scaled launch timeout: attributability only, not reliability. A 180s stall
      becomes a named error. Cheap and no-regret, but there is no stall to name.
  (c) shared launch helper: hygiene only. Deduplicating 51 call sites launches zero fewer
      browsers, because each file still needs its own context.

CORRECTION TO A PREMISE THIS BEAD REPEATS, also recorded on oculist-du2: the oculist-8ou
reviewer's 'all four launch options identical' claim is FALSE as stated. headless, channel
and args are identical across all 51 files; viewport is not (25x 1200x800, 22x 1280x800,
2x a VIEWPORT constant, 2x 1280x900), and a few files add colorScheme or reducedMotion.
Anyone sizing option (c) later needs a parameterised helper, not a zero-arg wrapper.

REOPEN IF: the suite fails on a solo npm test run, or if concurrent suite runs become a
requirement. If (b) is ever wanted purely for debuggability, it stands alone and does not
need this bead. See the test-suite-flake memory.

title: wizard_no_clinical_persistence.test.js has the same sticky gate at two sites, plus six fixed sleeps
description:
Found by the oculist-leu implementer and CONFIRMED against the code by the oculist-leu reviewer on 2026-09-02. Same defect class as oculist-leu, different file, deliberately not fixed there to keep that diff scoped.

THE FILE: test/wizard_no_clinical_persistence.test.js. It is a describe block whose tests share one browser context and one chrome.storage.sync blob, with no reset between them.

THE STICKY GATE. waitForSetupWizardCompleted polls the same predicate oculist-leu removed: stored.setupWizardCompleted, which goes true on the first wizard run and STAYS true. Per-site status, all verified by the reviewer rather than assumed:

  :95   test 1                    NOT vacuous. This is the first wizard run in the file, so storage is genuinely empty when it polls.
  :119  test 2                    VACUOUS. setupWizardCompleted is already true from test 1's write.
  :416  test 3, firstStored read  VACUOUS. Can read test 2's by-adjust / rose-cyan blob and then fail :417's high-contrast assertion.
  :485  test 3, secondStored read ALREADY CORRECT, leave it. It waits on wizard-modal display, which openWizard() flips back to flex on reopen and only sets to none after the write resolves, so it is genuinely non-sticky.

So two sites need fixing, not four. Do not 'fix' :95 or :485.

ALSO IN THIS FILE: six fixed-deadline sleeps, page.waitForTimeout(400) at :76, :89, :113, :407, :410 and :413. Same anti-pattern oculist-leu replaced. Bundle them here rather than filing a third bead.

DONE WHEN: the two vacuous polls can no longer return a previous test's state, and the six sleeps are replaced by real signals.

DIRECTION, and the reasoning is already settled so do not relitigate it. oculist-leu chose RESET over a per-case signal, and the reviewer's argument for that was: gating a poll on the value you are about to assert collapses the assertion into the wait predicate, making a pass tautological and a failure a bare timeout instead of a field-level diff. Reset keeps the poll a liveness gate and the assertion a correctness gate. The same logic applies here. See oculist-leu's close notes and 5529bd4 for the working pattern, including resetStoredSettings() via chrome.storage.sync.remove on the service worker.

For the sleeps, oculist-leu's clickAndAdvance() is the model: welcome.js auto-advances via setTimeout(navigateNext, 300), and the honest wait is the next step's .active class, since '.wizard-step.active { display: flex }' (welcome.html:117) is the only rule that makes a step render.

VERIFY BY MUTATION, not by watching it go green. Make a write slow and make it land the wrong value, and confirm the tests FAIL both ways with a field-level message. A test that stops flaking by also stopping asserting is a net loss, which is the whole reason oculist-leu was filed. Run the file at least 5 times isolated plus the full suite.
close_reason: Reviewer PASS. resetStoredSettings() de-vacuums both sticky setupWizardCompleted polls; six fixed sleeps replaced by .active-class waits. Mutation-verified independently: slow write doubles duration, wrong values give field-level diffs. 4 isolated runs 10/10, suite 307/0.

title: OCULIST_TEST_TIMEOUT_SCALE misses Playwright's 30s default action timeout, and 51 of 58 files launch Chromium at concurrency 4
description:
Found by the oculist-67h reviewer on 2026-09-02. Two systemic findings behind the contention family, split out of oculist-67h so they can be fixed independently of that bead's per-test question.

FINDING 1: AN UNSCALED TIMEOUT BUDGET THE KNOB SILENTLY MISSES.

test/helpers/wait.js's OCULIST_TEST_TIMEOUT_SCALE scales POLL_TIMEOUT (5000ms) and LONG_TIMEOUT (15000ms). It does NOT touch Playwright's DEFAULT ACTION TIMEOUT of 30s, which governs every un-timeouted locator call. So on a contended box, raising the scale buys headroom for the suite's own polls while leaving the deepest budget fixed.

This is not theoretical. A previously unexplained 30.1s failure in dim_highlight.test.js was traced to exactly this: nothing in that file has a 30s budget (every wait uses POLL_TIMEOUT), so the 30s came from Playwright's default applying to page.locator(INPUT).fill(term) in addTerm and page.locator(CHIP_TERM).nth(i).click() in clickChip. An element failed ACTIONABILITY for 30 straight seconds, which is a categorically deeper stall than a poll expiring, and the scale knob could never have helped.

Note how cleanly the observed failure durations map onto the three budgets in play: 5s POLL_TIMEOUT, 17.3s against the 15s LONG_TIMEOUT, and 30.1s against the Playwright default. That mapping is the evidence the whole suite is uniformly slower under load, and that one third of it is outside the knob.

DONE WHEN: the Playwright default is driven from the same TIMEOUT_SCALE, most likely via context.setDefaultTimeout() wherever the context is created, so OCULIST_TEST_TIMEOUT_SCALE=3 actually scales every budget rather than two thirds of them. Verify by setting the scale and confirming the effective action timeout changes, not just the poll timeouts.

FINDING 2: THE SUITE CONTENDS WITH ITSELF.

51 of 58 test files call launchPersistentContext, and npm test runs at --test-concurrency=4. On an IDLE machine with nothing else running, this produced a launchPersistentContext Timeout 180000ms exceeded in beacon_fade_persistent_overlays.test.js:34, which cascaded into 2 cancelled tests (305 pass / 0 fail / 2 cancelled, 210.7s).

That matters because it refutes the theory that the flakiness was imported from parallel orchestration. It is intrinsic. Quiet-machine full runs measured 67s, 67s, 68s, 69s, 71s, 86s, 88s and 210s: a 3x spread on an idle machine with a tail that reaches outright failure.

DONE WHEN: a full run's duration variance on an idle machine is materially tightened and a browser launch no longer times out. Options to price rather than assume: lower --test-concurrency, give launchPersistentContext an explicit scaled timeout, or reduce how many files need their own browser.

BE CAREFUL WITH THE OBVIOUS FIX. Dropping concurrency is the easy lever but the test-suite-flake memory records concurrency 1 at 232-245s per run against roughly 67-95s at concurrency 4, so serializing costs about 3x on every run forever. Measure before committing to it, and note that finding 1 may buy much of the stability for free.

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
ANOTHER DISTINCT FAILURE MODE observed 2026-09-02, on an idle machine, during unrelated work (the oculist-abk build.js change, which no test loads):

  test/list_search.test.js:356, via evalInContentScript at :127
  cdpSession.send: Protocol error (Runtime.evaluate): Promise was collected

An immediate re-run returned 307 pass / 0 fail.

WHY IT IS WORTH RECORDING SEPARATELY: this is NOT timeout-shaped. It is a CDP-level error from the browser side, meaning the Runtime.evaluate promise was garbage-collected before it resolved. So the failure catalogue for this suite now spans at least four distinct shapes:

  5s     POLL_TIMEOUT expiry
  17.3s  against the 15s LONG_TIMEOUT
  30.1s  against Playwright's unscaled default action timeout
  180s   launchPersistentContext timeout
  1671ms AssertionError on stale shared state (oculist-leu)
  n/a    CDP 'Promise was collected'

That variety matters for how this bead is approached. A single lever (lower concurrency, or scaling one timeout) is unlikely to address all of them, and the CDP error in particular suggests browser-session pressure rather than a budget being too tight. Worth counting the distinct shapes before pricing a fix, so the chosen lever is matched to the dominant one rather than the most recently seen one.

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
WORST RUN YET, observed 2026-09-02 on an idle machine while landing the oculist-abk / 296.9 work:

  297 pass / 2 fail / 8 CANCELLED, duration 299762ms (5 minutes)

For comparison, runs on the same branch minutes before and after were 84.1s, 101.5s and 103.1s, all 307/0. So the spread on an idle machine now measured spans 67s to 300s, and the tail reaches 8 cancelled tests.

HONEST LIMITATION: I captured the counts but NOT the failing test names for that run, because it was not piped to a file. The immediately following run was clean, so the names are lost. Recording it anyway because the SHAPE is the useful part and it is the most severe instance seen: 8 cancellations alongside 2 failures is the cascade signature already recorded on this bead (a launchPersistentContext timeout takes down its own file and cancels queued siblings), not an isolated assertion failure.

WHY IT IS NOT ATTRIBUTED TO THE WORK IN FLIGHT: the only code change on that branch is build.js, which no test loads (grep -rl 'build.js' test/ returns nothing), and the other change was a markdown file in a different repository. The 307/0 runs bracketing it on the same tree support that.

This strengthens the case that the dominant failure mode here is browser-launch capacity rather than any individual test's timeout budget. A 5 minute wall time with 8 cancellations is not a test that needs a bigger poll timeout; it is a suite that cannot get the browsers it asked for.

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
FINDING 1 DONE in c8db638. Finding 2 split out as oculist-3sx. Reviewer PASS on finding 1's done-criteria, but it REFUTED the implementer's causal claim and that correction matters more than the fix.

THE FIX ITSELF. wait.js now wraps chromium.launchPersistentContext to set the context default from TIMEOUT_SCALE. Re-measured by the reviewer rather than trusted: scale unset gives 30005ms, scale 3 gives 90007ms, and a control that does not import wait.js stays at 30005ms, confirming the change is what moves the number. The deliberate scale-1 default of 30s survives, preserving the property that a genuine regression still surfaces quickly.

THE CLAIM THAT WAS WRONG, recorded so nobody prices finding 2 off it. The implementer ran five suites at 307/0, 75.4s to 77.3s, and concluded finding 1 'accounts for most or all of the instability'. That was structurally unsupportable, not merely unproven: AT SCALE 1 THE PATCH IS A NO-OP BY CONSTRUCTION (30000 * 1 = 30000, which is Playwright's own default) and npm test never sets OCULIST_TEST_TIMEOUT_SCALE. So every run it cited as evidence was made with the change inert.

THE A/B THAT SETTLED IT. The reviewer ran interleaved B/P/B/P/B/P full suites on an idle machine, baseline being HEAD's wait.js with oculist-leu's fix still in place:

  BASELINE  307/0/0  76456ms, 76058ms, 75381ms   mean 75.97s
  PATCHED   307/0/0  76667ms, 77163ms, 75999ms   mean 76.61s

Indistinguishable, with the patched set marginally slower. Whatever tightened the suite was oculist-leu and/or a quieter machine, not this change.

HONEST LIMIT IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: six clean runs also fail to REPRODUCE the instability, so they are weak evidence it is gone. The bead records a 67s to 300s spread; six 76s runs do not settle that. This is why oculist-3sx requires a load repro before its options are priced.

FINDING 2 IS STILL NEEDED. The severe modes are launch-capacity shaped (launchPersistentContext Timeout 180000ms, 8 cancelled, 300s wall, CDP 'Promise was collected'), and this patch runs AFTER launchPersistentContext resolves, so a launch that never returns is categorically outside its reach.

ALSO FILED: oculist-du2, because the monkeypatch's correctness rests on all 51 launcher files happening to import helpers/wait, and nothing enforces that. A file 52 would silently get an unscaled default with the suite still green.

title: wizard_low_vision_palette_overlay.test.js asserts on the previous case's settings: its completion gate is sticky
description:
Found by the oculist-67h reviewer on 2026-09-02, reproduced on an IDLE machine (306 pass / 1 fail, the failure taking 1671ms, not a timeout). This is a real test defect, distinct from the contention family, and it is wrong by construction rather than merely flaky.

THE SITE: test/wizard_low_vision_palette_overlay.test.js:128.

THE SHAPE. The file runs 8 wizard cases against ONE SHARED chrome.storage.sync blob and never resets it between cases. Its completion gate is

  (stored) => !!(stored && stored.setupWizardCompleted)

setupWizardCompleted goes true in case 1 and STAYS true for the rest of the run. So for cases 2 through 8 that poll is VACUOUS: it returns immediately with whatever happens to be stored at that instant, which may still be the previous case's data. The test then asserts on it.

OBSERVED: the failing value was colorPalette 'amber-sky', which is exactly CASES[5]'s expected blob. The test asserted on the PRECEDING case's persisted settings before its own write had landed. It passes only when the write happens to be fast, which is why it looks like flake.

COMPOUNDING IT: the same file uses await page.waitForTimeout(400) as its step-advance. That is precisely the 'racing a fixed deadline' anti-pattern, and this repo has fixed the same class before under oculist-d5c (fusing a wait and its read into one page-side tick).

DONE WHEN: cases 2 through 8 can no longer read case N-1's state. Two directions, pick on the merits: reset oc-settings between cases so each starts from a known blank, or gate on a PER-CASE signal instead of the sticky setupWizardCompleted (for instance a value unique to the case being written). Also replace the waitForTimeout(400) step-advance with a real signal.

VERIFY BY MUTATION, do not just watch it go green: make the write deliberately slow or land the wrong palette and confirm the test FAILS. A test that stops flaking by also stopping asserting is a net loss. Run the file repeatedly (at least 5 times) plus the full suite.

ADJACENT, ONE LINE, NOT CHASED: test/wizard_no_clinical_persistence.test.js:66 uses the identical sticky setupWizardCompleted predicate plus six waitForTimeout sleeps, so it likely carries the same latent stale-read. Check it while you are in here; file separately if it is a real second instance.

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
Closed in 5529bd4 on epic/oculist-bead-loop. Reviewer PASS, first pass. npm test 307 pass / 0 fail; the file itself 8/8 across five isolated runs by the implementer and three more by the reviewer.

RESOLUTION: reset oc-settings before each case rather than gating on a per-case signal. The reviewer endorsed the choice and supplied a stronger argument than the implementer's own: gating the poll on the case's expected value would COLLAPSE THE ASSERTION INTO THE WAIT PREDICATE, so a pass becomes tautological and a failure surfaces as a bare timeout instead of a field-level deepStrictEqual diff. Reset keeps the poll a liveness gate and the assertion a correctness gate. The cost argument is one-sided too: storage.sync.remove is a few ms against roughly 2.6s per case.

The waitForTimeout(400) step-advance is gone, replaced by a wait on the next step's .active class. Verified that is a real signal rather than a differently-shaped race: showStep() toggles the class (welcome.js:293-298) and '.wizard-step.active { display: flex }' (welcome.html:117) is the only rule that makes a step render, so waitForSelector's default visible state waits on the actual transition.

MUTATIONS RE-RUN INDEPENDENTLY BY THE REVIEWER, not taken from the implementer:
- 6s delay around the writeOcSettings call: 0 pass / 8 fail, in two distinct modes (4 waitForCondition timeouts, 4 AssertionError mismatches).
- colorPalette forced to 'amber-sky': 2 pass / 6 fail. The claim that the 2 passes are CORRECT rather than a weakness was checked against the matrix: CASES:77-84 has exactly two entries expecting amber-sky (:78 and :82), and those are precisely the two that passed.

Reset confirmed to reach the right storage area empirically rather than by inspection: under mutation 1, case 1's poll reported its last observed value as {"disabledSites":["github.com"],"seededDefaultBlocklist":true}, so the blob was genuinely gone and only background.js's blocklist re-seed remained.

No assertion weakened: 2 assert calls before and after, byte-identical text. The waitForSelector count dropping 6 to 5 is textual only, three per-step waits collapsing into one call still executed three times.

ONE COMMENT CORRECTED BEFORE COMMIT. The new comment credited oculist-d5c with having fixed the 'hardcoded deadline' anti-pattern. False: d5c was a Node-side round trip letting a transient element self-clean between the wait and the read, and its commit 7ee36af removed ZERO waitForTimeout calls (verified: grep of that diff returns 0). Reworded to name the shared general move while stating plainly that d5c's specific defect was different.

Two follow-ups filed separately, both confirmed by the reviewer against the code rather than assumed.

title: HUMAN ONLY: tag and submit the folded Halloween release

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
DECISION REQUIRED BEFORE SUBMITTING, from oculist-296.3 (2026-09-02): does a reversible functional preset count as 'Health information' in the Chrome Web Store data-usage declarations?

The full argument both ways, with code citations and a recommendation, is written out in artifacts/outputs/store-submission-v1.7.0.md under 'FLAGGED FOR HUMAN CONFIRMATION: does a reversible functional preset count as Health information'. Read that, not this summary.

The short version. Oculist no longer stores the clinical label; it stores a functional preset. But the mapping is fixed and total (LEGACY_DISPLAY_PRESET_MAP, Object.freeze'd, six entries, all values distinct), and popup.js:113-116 inverts it, so a synced 'rg-adjust-deut' reconstructs 'color-blind-deuteranopia' deterministically. But it is closer to the line than earlier listing versions, and it is your call, not an agent's.

The oculist-296.3 reviewer found a second reversible channel: colorPalette maps 1:1 onto the same three conditions (welcome.js:68-90 stores amber-sky for deuteranopia, amber-indigo for protanopia, rose-cyan for tritanopia), it lives in visionSettings, and visionSettings is in SETTINGS_KEYS so it syncs. The two are independent: per welcome.js:136-137 a low-vision user who also answers the color question syncs displayPreset 'high-contrast' PLUS a palette that still reveals the color condition, so masking displayPreset alone would not close the inference. A 'Yes' also means PRIVACY.md needs a matching update.

The other flagged question in the same doc, whether saved search-term lists count as 'website content' or 'user activity', is unrelated and predates this run. It also recommends not ticking either. Both need your answer before the dashboard form can be completed.

title: Re-verify the store listing copy against what v1.7.0 actually ships
description:

comments.text:

The expected outcome was a clean no-op. It was not: one real defect in the Health information disclosure, plus a stale citation inside the very paragraph documenting it.

title: trail_effect.test.js asserts on transient beacon/flash elements after waitForSelector has already returned, so they can self-clean before the read
description:
Found by the oculist-a4f reviewer on 2026-09-01, reproduced in a single npm test run (305 pass / 2 fail, 86.7s, on a clean tree at 3b4971d).

This is a REAL TEST DEFECT, distinct from the --test-concurrency=4 contention timeouts that a4f was filed about. Both families hit the same file, which is why they were conflated for so long.

THE SHAPE: replay() at test/trail_effect.test.js:207 does waitForSelector('.oc-trail-arrow') and SUCCEEDS. Milliseconds later the test counts the element and it is already gone - the transient effect completed and self-cleaned in between. Same at :546: waitForSelector(FLASH) succeeds, then querySelector('.oc-trail-flash') at :548 returns null.

OBSERVED FAILURES (note they are FAST - 159ms and 912ms - not 5000ms timeouts, which is the discriminator against the contention family):
- :422 'Lite Mode drops the trailing line, keeping only the arrowhead' -> AssertionError 'full mode must render the arrowhead', 0 !== 1, strictEqual, at :425
- :544 'the absorption flash runs exactly one iteration (WCAG 2.3.1 guard)' -> page.evaluate TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'getAnimations') at :548

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE NOISE: :544 is the WCAG 2.3.1 guard (no strobe/loop). A flaky accessibility guard gets ignored and then stops catching a real seizure-risk regression. That was a4f's original P3 rationale and it applies more sharply here, because this family is a defect rather than contention.

LIKELY ALSO EXPLAINS a4f's long-unattributed baseline failure. :415 does assert.ok((await page.locator('.oc-beacon').count()) > 0, 'sanity check: the beacon must actually render before checking it is cleaned up'). assert.ok(false, msg) in Node reports exactly 'AssertionError actual:false expected:true, operator ==' - the signature a4f recorded on an untouched baseline and could never name.

AFFECTED SITES, at least: :415, :425, :548.

DONE WHEN: these assertions no longer depend on a transient element surviving between the wait that observed it and the read that measures it. Raising a timeout is explicitly NOT the fix - the failures are fast, so OCULIST_TEST_TIMEOUT_SCALE has no effect on them. Likely direction: capture the observation and the measurement in the SAME page-side evaluate, so there is no Node-side round trip during which the element can vanish. Verify the fixed assertions still FAIL when the behavior under test is genuinely broken - a test that stops vanishing by also stopping asserting is a net loss.

See the test-suite-flake memory (key test-suite-flake-npm-test-runs-at-test) for the two-family split and the discriminator.

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
Caveat from the a4f re-reviewer, add to the analysis before fixing: this bead frames the vanishing element as a TEST-timing artifact, but the element disappearing could itself be a PRODUCT-side defect (an early fade or cancel). Do not fix by making the test tolerate the disappearance until you have established which it is - that would mask a real bug. The 'must still FAIL when the behavior under test is broken' clause partially covers this, but establish the cause first. Note oculist-1rf's analysis already ruled out ONE candidate: fadeActiveBeacons() (content.js:5210-5242) captures a STATIC NodeList and only touches captured elements, so a stale fade timer from an earlier case cannot remove a later case's beacon.

Cosmetic correction to this bead's text: :548 is the page.evaluate call line (what the stack trace reports); the querySelector itself is at :549-550.

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
Fixed in 7ee36af on epic/oculist-d5c-rnr8. title: fadeActiveBeacons wipes the persistent accessibility overlays, not just the transient beacon
description:
Reviewer finding during oculist-9t5, verified by execution. Pre-existing for full motion; oculist-9t5 extended its blast radius to reduced motion.

fadeActiveBeacons() (extension/content.js, called from handleScroll) fades and removes EVERY .oc-beacon element. But drawActiveOverlays() classes the persistent accessibility overlays as .oc-beacon too - the border (around :3262), the shape (:3297), the label (:3325) and the magnifier card (:3439). So the first scroll after a match wipes them all, not just the transient beacon effect.

Measured with borderStyle 'thick': full motion, before=2 after=0 - already the behaviour today. Reduced motion, before=2 after=2 before oculist-9t5, before=2 after=0 after it. So 9t5 did not create this bug, it made reduced motion consistent with full motion, which is the direction 9t5 wanted for the transient beacon and the wrong direction for these overlays.

Why it is the wrong direction: unlike the transient beacon, these overlays are positioned in DOCUMENT coordinates and track scroll correctly. They are not stale, they are not misleading, and they are the high-visibility affordance the whole product exists to provide. Fading them on scroll is pure loss, and it lands hardest on exactly the users who turned a thick border on.

FIX: the fade query is too broad. Tag the transient beacon elements distinctly - a second class such as oc-beacon-transient on what the effects draw - and have fadeActiveBeacons() select only those, leaving the persistent overlays alone. cancelBeacons() should keep clearing everything, since a new search legitimately tears the whole set down. Check every place that creates a .oc-beacon and decide per site which category it is; animateReducedMotion draws BOTH kinds (a transient glow and, under displayPreset reduced-motion, an arrows+spotlight overlay), so it needs care.

Do not simply exclude the overlays by their own class names - that is a fourth list to keep in sync with drawActiveOverlays. One positive marker on the transient elements is the maintainable version.

TEST: with borderStyle 'thick', run a search, scroll, and assert the border overlay survives while the transient beacon is gone. Cover both full and reduced motion.

Verify all line references against current files before acting.

title: speed_lines.test.js 'survives a scroll between capture and read' now fails: fadeActiveBeacons correctly fades/removes the beacon on real scroll, so speedLinesDone never fires
description:
test/speed_lines.test.js's 'the centre-line highlight anchor check survives a scroll between capture and read' test (around line 446) fails as a direct, correct consequence of the oculist-qii fix.

Root cause: this test does window.scrollTo(0, SCROLL_AT_CAPTURE), fires the beacon, then window.scrollTo(0, SCROLL_AT_READ) while the beacon is still live, and then waits for window.__ocTest.speedLinesDone to become true. Before oculist-qii, fadeActiveBeacons() (content.js, called from handleScroll() on every 'scroll' event) already faded and removed the .oc-beacon element ~50ms after any scroll, but it did NOT cancel the animateSpeedLines() rAF loop — the loop kept running on the orphaned, detached canvas until it reached its own natural completion (t >= 1), which is what set speedLinesDone = true. The test's "wait for speedLinesDone" only ever passed because of that leak.

oculist-qii fixed exactly this: fadeActiveBeacons() now goes through the same destroyBeacon() helper as cancelBeacons(), so it cancels container.__rafId (and any __waapiAnims) atomically with removal. After the fix, the second scrollTo() in this test genuinely fades and removes the beacon and cancels its rAF loop, so the loop never reaches its completion branch and speedLinesDone never becomes true — the test times out (15s) waiting for it.

This is not a flake and not a regression in the fix; it's an existing test whose premise (a beacon can be scrolled mid-flight and still reach natural completion) is no longer true now that scrolling correctly cancels beacons. The test's real intent, per its own name/history (oculist-viv), is to verify that the centre-line highlight's document-coordinate math stays correct across an intervening scroll — not to test whether a beacon survives a scroll.

Needs a design decision on how to restructure this test now that "scroll mid-flight" and "beacon still animating" are mutually exclusive:
- Read the anchor value at a moment before the 50ms fade-removal window closes (i.e. immediately after the second scrollTo(), before the fade timer fires), instead of waiting for speedLinesDone.
- Or add a test-only escape hatch (e.g. exposing a way to force isAutoScrolling true) so the scroll doesn't trigger fadeActiveBeacons() — mirrors real auto-scroll navigation, but changes what the test actually exercises.
- Or pick two scroll positions during which the effect legitimately completes before any scroll fires (removes the "between capture and read" scroll entirely) and cover the coordinate-math regression a different way.

Verified by running the full suite after the oculist-qii fix: 284 passing, 1 failing (this test) out of 285 total (283 baseline + 2 new oculist-qii tests). Not the known stale_mount_guard flake.
close_reason: Closed

title: fadeActiveBeacons removes beacons without cancelling their rAF loop
description:
Reviewer finding during oculist-3ae. Pre-existing, affects EVERY canvas effect, and it is the root cause blocking oculist-3ae.

extension/content.js's fadeActiveBeacons() (around :4957, called from handleScroll) removes .oc-beacon elements but never cancels container.__rafId. cancelBeacons() (around :1024-1042) does cancel-then-remove; fadeActiveBeacons() only removes.

Consequence: any scroll during a live beacon detaches the container while its requestAnimationFrame loop is still scheduled. The loop keeps running against a detached canvas, and because cancelBeacons() finds its targets via document.querySelectorAll('.oc-beacon'), the detached container is permanently unreachable - nothing can ever cancel it. The loop only stops when it reaches its own completion branch.

Reproduced 2/2 with a real page.mouse.wheel mid-beacon; 0/1 without the scroll. Instrumented trace: 'fadeActiveBeacons activeBeacons=1' -> container removed at frame 23 -> loop continues 25, 26 ... 32 -> later 'cancelBeacons n=0'.

Today this is mostly wasted work on a detached canvas. It becomes a crash the moment any effect's frame loop READS a property off a hook the next run can null - which is exactly what oculist-3ae's hook reset introduces for chrono's lastChronoHueRun.hueSamples.push. See the comment on oculist-3ae for the full trace.

FIX: make fadeActiveBeacons() cancel the same way cancelBeacons() does before removing - cancelAnimationFrame(container.__rafId) and clear __waapiAnims - rather than duplicating that logic, factor out the single teardown both call. Check every other place that removes a .oc-beacon for the same omission.

TEST: scroll during a live beacon and assert the effect's frame counter stops advancing after the removal. test/chrono_tunnel.test.js's 'no frame() runs after the beacon container is removed' case (on branch wip/oculist-3ae) is the shape to copy, driven by a real scroll instead of natural completion.

BLOCKS: oculist-3ae. Fixing this first lets 3ae land with no per-push null guards.

Verify all line references against current files before acting.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
HALTED on a stop condition: the fix turns the full suite red. Work preserved on branch wip/oculist-qii (commit effccfd), NOT on the epic branch. Do not merge as-is.

THE FIX ITSELF LOOKS RIGHT and is unreviewed only because the run halted before the reviewer was dispatched. It extracts destroyBeacon(b) - cancelAnimationFrame(__rafId) + cancel every __waapiAnims entry + remove() - out of cancelBeacons(), and calls it from fadeActiveBeacons()'s existing 50ms setTimeout in place of the bare .remove(). Cancelling at removal rather than at fade start is deliberate: during the fade the beacon is still attached and so still reachable by cancelBeacons(), and cancelling at fade start would freeze the canvas mid-fade.

BLOCKER: test/speed_lines.test.js 'the centre-line highlight anchor check survives a scroll between capture and read' (around :446) now times out at 15s. Suite is 284 pass / 1 fail. See oculist-a96 for the full analysis.

Short version: that test scrolls to SCROLL_AT_CAPTURE, fires the beacon, scrolls to SCROLL_AT_READ while it is still live, then waits for window.__ocTest.speedLinesDone === true. Pre-fix, the second scroll made fadeActiveBeacons() detach the beacon but leave its rAF loop running, and the orphaned loop ran on to its natural completion branch, which is what set speedLinesDone. The wait only ever succeeded because of the bug this bead fixes. Post-fix the loop is genuinely cancelled, so speedLinesDone never fires.

The test's real intent is worth keeping: it checks that lastSpeedLinesContainerRect is captured in document coordinates, so a scroll between capture and read cannot corrupt the anchor. That assertion is still valid; only its 'wait for natural completion' mechanism is not.

NEEDS A HUMAN CALL - how should that coverage be preserved?
(A) Stop waiting for speedLinesDone. Read lastSpeedLinesHighlightY and lastSpeedLinesContainerRect right after the scroll, off the frames the test already waited for (it polls speedLinesFrameCount >= 2 before scrolling). Keeps the anchor assertion, drops the dependency on completion. Looks like the cleanest fit to me, but it does mean the test no longer exercises a full run end to end.
(B) Move the scroll to after completion. Preserves the end-to-end run but stops testing 'scroll BETWEEN capture and read', which is the whole point of the test's name.
(C) Have the test suppress the fade for its own duration (e.g. drive the scroll without a scroll event, or restore the beacon). Keeps both properties but adds test-only machinery to work around real product behaviour.

ALSO FOUND, not yet its own bead - decide whether it warrants one: drawActiveMatchLabel (around :3321) and drawActiveMatchMagnifier (around :3384) each do a bare existing.remove() to replace a previous same-id overlay while its __waapiAnims may still be running (a 250ms label fade, an up-to-470ms magnifier lift). Same omission this bead fixes, different call sites, and neither is one of the effects' own completion self-removals. They should probably go through destroyBeacon() too.

AUDIT RESULT for the record: cancelBeacons() and fadeActiveBeacons() are the only two general teardown paths and both now route through the helper. Every effect's own completion self-removal (chrono ~:2811, speedlines ~:2631, and the WAAPI effects) was reported and deliberately left alone - cancelling from those setTimeout(DUR) timers kills the legitimate final frame, as disproven by execution during oculist-3ae. Those belong to oculist-3ae and oculist-ws4.

TEST NOTE worth keeping: the two new tests needed document.body.style.paddingBottom = '2000px' because the existing fixture pages are exactly one viewport tall, so a wheel scroll was a no-op and the tests passed for the wrong reason until that was added.

title: isOculistNode/isOculistMutation ignores text-node mutations and beacon-descendant elements, causing spurious background rescans (e.g. Cyber-Vision's readout textContent write)
description:
Found while implementing oculist-3ae. content.js's isOculistNode() (used by isOculistMutation() to filter the finder's own DOM writes out of the debounced MutationObserver rescan) only recognizes:
- the wrap element itself / #oc-wrap / #oc-global-highlight-styles
- Element nodes (nodeType 1) carrying the oc-beacon or oc-viewport-marker class

It does NOT recognize:
1. Text nodes at all (nodeType 3) -- isOculistNode() returns false unconditionally for any text node, even one added as a child of an oculist-owned element.
2. Beacon-descendant elements that don't themselves carry the oc-beacon/oc-viewport-marker class -- e.g. Cyber-Vision's readout div (class oc-cv-readout), a child of the .oc-beacon container.

Concretely: animateCyberVision() sets `readout.textContent = ...`, which creates a text-node child of the readout div. Since neither the readout element nor its new text-node child is recognized as "oculist" by isOculistNode(), isOculistMutation() returns false for this mutation, and startDomObserver()'s callback schedules a genuine rescanAfterMutation() 350ms later on every single Cyber-Vision run.

Impact: if the active match happens to become invisible (e.g. zero-size, display:none) within that 350ms window, the spurious rescan's performListSearch()/findRanges() call filters the match out as invisible and wipes searchRanges to empty ("no match"), even though nothing about the page's real content changed. Confirmed via a temporary diagnostic patch to startDomObserver() while building oculist-3ae's cyber_vision.test.js "stale timer" test -- see that test's forceMatchRediscovery() helper, which works around the gap by forcing a genuine (non-oculist) childList mutation to trigger a real recovery rescan, since a plain style restore is only an attribute change the observer never even sees (it's registered with {childList:true, subtree:true} only).

Fix should generalize isOculistNode() to also recognize:
- text nodes whose parentElement is itself an oculist node (or a similar ancestor-walk), and/or
- elements whose class list starts with oc-cv-/oc- or whose closest oc-beacon ancestor exists

Out of scope for oculist-3ae (which is specifically about the __ocTest hook-reset-before-guard gap in animateChronoTunnel/animateCyberVision), since this is a pre-existing, unrelated MutationObserver filtering gap.
close_reason: Closed

title: seedDefaultBlocklist can erase the welcome wizard's own settings write on first install
description:
Found by the oculist-8s5 reviewer, 2026-08-31, while root-causing a test flake. This is a PRODUCT bug, not a test artifact. Reproduced 5 times in 40 runs.

MECHANISM:
extension/background.js updateSettings() (lines 124-144) does get -> mutate -> set with no compare-and-swap. seedDefaultBlocklist() runs from onInstalled; on a fresh profile its get() snapshots {} BEFORE a concurrent page/popup/wizard write lands, and its set() commits AFTER, erasing that write.

Observed storage state at the moment of failure:
  {"disabledSites":["github.com"],"seededDefaultBlocklist":true}
That is exactly the seed mutation applied to an empty snapshot. The concurrent write, an effect selection, was gone entirely: the key was ABSENT, not stale.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A NARROW RACE:
1. The clobber window coincides with chrome.tabs.create(welcome.html), which background.js opens on the line above. So the setup wizard is launched INSIDE the window in which anything it writes can be silently erased.
2. It does not self-correct. content.js's storage.onChanged handler guards per key with 'if (!(k in nv)) return;' (content.js:7217). The clobbering payload carries no 'effect' key, so an already-open tab keeps its in-memory value forever and never notices. The loss only surfaces on the NEXT page load, in a fresh tab.
3. The wizard tab itself still looks correct while open, because its own state is in memory. The user sees their choice applied, then finds it gone later.
4. Measured window is multi-second under load, not milliseconds. The write happened roughly 1-2s after launch and was still erased.

WHEN IT FIRES: only while seededDefaultBlocklist is falsy, i.e. first install, and an update from a pre-seeding build. That is precisely the moment the wizard runs.

PRIOR ART: oculist-9s9 fixed the background-vs-background case by sequencing both onInstalled writes through one updateSettings(). The comment at background.js:116-123 explicitly documents this remaining background-vs-PAGE window as un-closeable without a CAS primitive chrome.storage does not offer. That is true of CAS specifically, but the bug is still MITIGABLE:
  (a) skip the set() entirely when the mutation changes nothing (the seed already returns false when seededDefaultBlocklist is set; extend that to a genuine no-op check), and/or
  (b) defer seeding until after the welcome tab has been created and had a chance to write, and/or
  (c) re-read and merge immediately before set() rather than writing a snapshot taken earlier.

Verify all line references against the current file before acting; background.js changed under oculist-9s9 and oculist-hzr.

Related: oculist-9s9 (closed), oculist-hzr (closed), oculist-8s5 (the flake this surfaced through).
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
Discovered through the oculist-8s5 flake investigation and confirmed as its root cause.

The test-side workaround is committed as 1145a5d on epic/fix-oculist-8s5: test/trail_effect.test.js now forces the effect via the setEffectKey test hook instead of relying on a storage read. That makes the test deterministic but DOES NOT fix this bug, and it removes the only signal the suite currently had for it. Nothing else in the suite would notice this erasure.

That trade is deliberate and recorded, not an oversight: the trail test guards keyboard-only path anchoring, not settings persistence, and the erasure threatens every test that writes settings early. But it does mean this bead is now the only thing tracking the defect.

Reproduction method if it is needed again: run test/trail_effect.test.js repeatedly under CPU load against the tree before 1145a5d, and read chrome.storage.sync from the new tab's isolated world at the moment the assertion fails. 5 hits in 40 runs, every hit showing the same stored object with the effect key absent entirely.

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD'S PREMISE, and the fix that landed.

I filed this bead and its headline scenario was WRONG. Both the implementer and the reviewer independently confirmed from the code: chrome.tabs.create({url: welcome.html}) sits INSIDE seedDefaultBlocklist's done callback, and done is only reached from a set callback (already committed) or the skip path (nothing pending). The wizard tab therefore cannot open until after the seed's write has landed, so the wizard's own write can never race the seed's get-to-set window. 'seedDefaultBlocklist can erase the welcome wizard's own settings write' is unreachable as stated.

The concern was aimed one write site early rather than fabricated: on low-core installs the performanceMode write runs AFTER the wizard tab opens, so THAT write genuinely could race the wizard's write. The fix now recovers it.

THE REAL EXPOSURE, per the reviewer:
- Racers are the <all_urls> document_idle content script (content.js:71 saveSettings does a bare storage.sync.set), popup.js:195/395, and welcome.js:833. None had equivalent protection.
- On INSTALL: low. Chrome does not retro-inject declarative content scripts into already-open tabs and the popup is not open at that instant. Only a page finishing navigation inside the same few-ms window.
- On UPDATE: materially higher, and this is the real case. Live tabs exist, freshly navigated ones inject the new content.js immediately, and the seed still performs a full write on the one update from a pre-seeding build. After that the flag makes mutate return false and no set happens at all, so the hazard is one-shot per profile.
- Severity stays P2 despite the lower likelihood: the loss is silent and PERMANENT, because content.js:7217's 'if (!(k in nv)) return;' means an erased key produces no onChanged entry, so the tab keeps its stale in-memory value and never rewrites it.

FIXED IN 5c2f5b9 with confirm-then-retry optimistic concurrency in updateSettings: re-read and compare against the snapshot mutate ran on, re-run mutate against fresh state on drift, bounded to 3 attempts by observed drift rather than elapsed time. On exhaustion it writes the freshest recomputation, degrading to the old last-writer-wins rather than to data loss. Reviewer verified done fires exactly once across all eight paths, the retry cannot loop, and seed-once semantics survive retries.

title: Four contention flakes make the release gate non-deterministic
description:
Reviewer finding across oculist-rnr.12/.13/.15/.17. Over this epic, npm test rarely produced a clean full run on the first try; the release-gate verification for rnr.17 needed three runs plus an isolation run to establish green.

Four suites fail intermittently under concurrency, all confirmed passing in isolation:
- test/speed_lines.test.js:336 'Lite Mode still draws the centre-line highlight on every frame' (frame-count off by one or two). Tracked separately as oculist-vuk.
- test/trail_effect.test.js:277
- test/worklist_storage.test.js (chrome.storage.session write timeout, 15s)
- test/stale_mount_guard.test.js:176 (waitForFunction 5000ms timeout)

Isolation run of all four together: 26 tests, 26 pass, 0 fail. So these are contention under --test-concurrency=4, not real failures.

Cost: every review in this epic had to re-run and reason about whether a failure was real, which is exactly the judgment a release gate should not require. A gate that cries wolf trains people to wave failures through.

Steps:
1. Identify what the four contend for. Likely candidates: a shared browser instance, real-time frame counting under CPU load, and fixed timeouts sized for an idle machine.
2. Prefer fixing the contention over adding retries. oculist-l6m.32 already converted 106 fixed sleeps to condition polling for this same class of problem; these four look like the residue.
3. Frame-count assertions (speed_lines, trail_effect) should assert a range or a monotonic property, not an exact count, since exact frame counts are wall-clock dependent by nature.
4. If serialization is the answer, mark just these suites rather than dropping concurrency for the whole run.
5. Prove it: run the full suite ten times and require ten clean passes.

Related: oculist-66m (vacuous waitForFunction predicates) touches the same files and should probably be done first or together.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: ya8282
comments.text:
Another data point from the oculist-rnr.19 review (2026-08-30). Across 21 executions on this branch the reviewer saw one failure of the NEW wizard arrow-key test: 4th assertion, '-1' !== '0' — focus had moved and aria-selected had flipped on the sample tab, but its tabindex was still the static -1.

That state is unreachable from the source: the aria-selected and tabindex writes are adjacent lines in the same synchronous forEach. The observed output is byte-identical to a deliberate mutation probe that DELETED the tabindex line, which points at the page having run a stale welcome.js rather than at a logic race.

Corroborating: the same run also flaked speed_lines.test.js, stale_mount_guard.test.js and worklist_storage.test.js, all files untouched by that diff. Isolated runs of the wizard file were 17/17 green, including 12 under 6-way CPU contention.

Reading: environmental (degraded machine and/or a stale extension asset), consistent with this bead's contention-flake thesis. A stale-asset mechanism would be a distinct cause from pure timing contention and may be worth separating out if it recurs.

title: Answering yes to both colour blindness and low vision drops the colour choice
description:
Found by the reviewer during oculist-rnr.13. PRE-EXISTING, not caused by that bead.

In the onboarding wizard, a user who answers yes to a colour-vision question AND yes to low vision loses their colour selection entirely: choosing amber-indigo plus low-vision persists displayPreset 'high-contrast' with colorPalette 'default'. The colour palette they picked is discarded.

This affects exactly the users with the most need, those with more than one vision difference, and it is silent - nothing tells them their colour choice was dropped.

Steps:
1. Reproduce: run the wizard, pick a colour option in step 1 and yes in the low-vision step, then inspect the persisted oc-settings.
2. Decide the correct semantics. Most likely the low-vision preset should compose WITH the chosen palette (sizing and contrast from one, palette from the other) rather than replace it. Confirm the intended behaviour before coding, since this is product semantics.
3. Fix the preset resolution so both answers contribute.
4. Add a test covering every combination of colour answer and low-vision answer.
close_reason: Closed

title: Several tests use waitForFunction predicates that never block
description:
Discovered during oculist-rnr.12 by comparing against a stashed pre-change baseline. Pre-existing, not caused by that bead.

Several *.test.js files check storage writes with a pattern shaped like:
  waitForFunction(() => chrome.storage.sync.get(...).then(d => !!(...)))
The predicate returns a PROMISE, which is always truthy, so waitForFunction resolves immediately on the first poll regardless of whether the underlying condition ever became true. The assertion silently passes even when the value was never written.

Impact: an unknown number of existing storage-write assertions are vacuous. They would not catch a regression in the code they appear to guard. This weakens the suite in exactly the area (settings and list persistence) that the v1.7.0 work depends on.

Steps:
1. Grep test/ for waitForFunction calls whose callback body contains .then( or returns a promise.
2. For each, rewrite to await the storage read and assert on the resolved value, or make the predicate synchronous over already-fetched state, matching whatever pattern the correct tests in the suite already use.
3. Confirm each rewritten assertion FAILS when the behaviour it guards is deliberately broken. A test that cannot fail is not a test.

Do not bulk-rewrite without checking each one - some may be correct already.
close_reason: Closed

title: Marketing site never mentions multi-term lists, v1.7.0's headline feature
description:
